title: Harsha slams Budget 2027 for being ‘too traditional’ | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 04:05
-     - 42

SJB MP Dr. Harsha de Silva yesterday quoting the Daily FT during his speech at the Budget 2027 debate in Parliament

Delivering the much-anticipated Opposition response to the Government’s Budget 2027 yesterday, Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) MP Dr. Harsha de Silva slammed the Government of failing to think beyond traditional solutions, not providing relief at household level, and called for policies to build an asset-owning population and to protect borrowers from losing their assets to banks. 

Speaking in the Budget 2027 debate in Parliament, Dr. de Silva said asset ownership was what set the SJB apart from the Government. “Mr. Speaker, the difference between us and them is very clear. We want to create an asset-owning population,” he said.

He questioned why the Government had not considered employee share ownership, including at State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs). “Why didn’t you think about an employee shareholdership program?” he asked.

Dr. de Silva welcomed a Budget move to introduce schoolchildren to the stock market and said it should have been done earlier. But he said the SJB wanted to go further, with Sri Lankans owning shares in global companies such as Tesla, Nvidia and Microsoft. “That is the asset-owning democracy we believe in,” he said.

Turning to parate execution, which allows banks to auction property mortgaged against defaulted loans without going to court, Dr. de Silva said borrowers who ran into difficulty should not be stripped of all their assets.

“A farmer starting a business does not mean that he has to give up everything he has and become bankrupt,” he said.

He said businesses needed a restructuring mechanism similar to Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US, under which a company keeps control of its assets while it restructures its debts. He said this had been agreed with Parliament’s Finance Committee but had not been implemented, leaving borrowers’ land at risk of being taken over. 

Had the Government thought out of the box and set up a credit guarantee corporation, the amounts owed could have been settled within three or four quarters, he said. He added that the Government had promised to set up a development bank, but it was not in the Budget.

Dr. de Silva also called for a dedicated housing finance institution. He said Colombo was among the least affordable cities in the world for buying a home and that small loans still carried high interest rates. “Why don’t you think of a housing finance institution? You are so traditional,” he said. He cited Freddie Mac in the US and similar institutions in India, and warned that the problem could not be solved with “traditional tricks”.

He also called for the interest on housing loans and health insurance premiums to be made deductible from taxable income.

On revenue, he said cigarette taxes had not been set against a global benchmark. He also questioned the taxation of online casinos when the country had no casino regulator.

Dr. de Silva accused the Government of starting new initiatives instead of implementing the Economic Transformation Act. “Why don’t you implement the Economic Transformation Act? Why reinvent this? There is no need to reinvent the wheel,” he said. He said Sri Lanka did not have a single private investment zone. Under the Budget, zones would come through the Board of Investment (BOI), while India, Thailand and Vietnam had many such zones, he said.

On agriculture, he urged the Government to help small farmers build strong brands for their produce. “Don’t be patronising. Don’t think that you know better than the farmers,” he said, adding that the issue concerned the two million families engaged in agriculture.

Dr. de Silva said the Budget offered little for young people, as artificial intelligence (AI) eroded software, internship and accounting jobs. “Yes, we are talking about giving a little here, giving a little there. But where is your grand plan? What are you going to do for Gen Z? What are you going to do for the lower-age millennials?” he asked.

He said the International Monetary Fund (IMF) program would end in March 2027 and the Government needed to decide on the way forward. He also questioned how a Marxist party that had been anti-IMF in the past was now pro-IMF. Dr. de Silva further said the Government’s tax policies were worsening protein deficiency among vulnerable groups.

He ended by citing economist Prof. Premachandra Athukorala, who has described Sri Lanka as a land of missed opportunities. “We have to have a vision. We have to have a team. We need a path, and we will build that path,” Dr. de Silva said.

title: Rs. 461 b forgone on indirect taxes alone in 1H 2026 | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 04:03
-     - 29

The Government gave up Rs. 796 billion in indirect tax revenue through exemptions, waivers and concessionary rates in 2025, with Value Added Tax (VAT) reliefs accounting for more than half, official data showed.

The Tax Expenditure Statement 2025/2026, issued by the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry on 12 November, 2026 under the Public Financial Management Act, No. 44 of 2024, put VAT reliefs at Rs. 419 billion last year.

Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL) reliefs cost Rs. 216 billion, Customs Import Duty (CID) reliefs Rs. 144 billion and Excise Duty (Special Provisions) reliefs Rs. 16 billion.

The cost has continued to mount in 2026. Indirect tax reliefs reached Rs. 461 billion in the first half of the year. VAT reliefs rose 17.2% to Rs. 243 billion from Rs. 207 billion in the same period of 2025, while SSCL reliefs amounted to Rs. 135 billion, CID reliefs Rs. 74 billion and excise reliefs Rs. 9 billion.

Direct tax reliefs, which are reported by year of assessment, also rose sharply. Corporate Income Tax (CIT) reliefs increased 56% to Rs. 186 billion in 2024/25 from Rs. 119 billion in 2023/24, mainly because of higher concessions and exemptions granted to non-BOI companies, excluding Port City projects, and to BOI projects. Concessionary tax rates for non-BOI companies alone cost Rs. 107 billion.

Personal Income Tax (PIT) reliefs more than tripled to Rs. 36 billion from Rs. 10.5 billion. Exempted and excluded income made up Rs. 32 billion, or 89.2% of the total.

The Ministry measures each relief as the gap between the tax actually payable and the tax that would have been due under the standard rules, but warned against reading the figures as money the Treasury could easily recover. “Accordingly, a tax expenditure estimate should not be interpreted as an estimate of the revenue that would necessarily be realised if the relevant provisions were abolished,” the statement said.

Among Customs reliefs, waivers under Section 19A of the Customs Ordinance cost Rs. 131 billion, or 91% of the total, as petrol and diesel imports rose 5.4%.

Excise reliefs were driven almost entirely by locally assembled vehicles, which accounted for Rs. 16 billion, or 99.4%. The number of locally assembled vehicles rose 74.2% to 96,472 in 2025 from 55,377 in 2024.

On the Luxury Tax on Motor Vehicles, the Department of Motor Traffic and Sri Lanka Customs are recovering concessions from permit holders who failed to register their vehicles by 30 September, 2024, as directed by the Committee on Public Accounts. As a result, the 2024 estimate was revised to Rs. 1.8 billion from Rs. 1.9 billion, and the number of beneficiaries to 662 from 721.

The Ministry acknowledged the scale of support provided through the tax system. “While such measures may serve legitimate policy objectives, they reduce or defer Government revenue and may therefore represent a significant, though less visible, form of public support,” the statement said.

It also conceded that the cost of a relief is only part of the picture. “The fiscal cost of a measure is one important consideration, but a comprehensive assessment should also consider its effectiveness, beneficiaries, distributional impact, economic effects, administrative and compliance costs, behavioural responses and the availability of alternative policy instruments,” the Ministry said.

The Ministry said it would develop multi-year analysis of major reliefs, introduce analysis of who benefits across income groups, sectors, firm sizes and regions, and improve disclosure of aggregate information on beneficiaries, subject to confidentiality requirements. “The analysis underscores the importance of regularly monitoring tax expenditures, evaluating their policy effectiveness and ensuring that their fiscal costs are consistent with broader revenue mobilization objectives,” it said.

title: Former British High Commissioner joins George Steuart Board | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 04:03
-     - 32

Former British High Commissioner to Sri Lanka James Dauris, George Steuart Group Chairman Sarva Ameresekere

George Steuart and Company Ltd., yesterday announced the appointment of former British High Commissioner to Sri Lanka and the Maldives James Dauris as an Independent Non-Executive Director of its Board, with effect from 1 January 2027.



Dauris brings over three decades of experience spanning international diplomacy, commercial relations and strategic advisory. His distinguished career includes serving as British High Commissioner to Sri Lanka and the Maldives from 2015 to 2019, British Ambassador to Peru and Panama, and holding senior leadership positions within the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

A graduate in Law from the University of Cambridge, he began his professional career as a solicitor in London, specialising in corporate and commercial law, before entering diplomatic service. 

The appointment reinforces George Steuart and Company’s British heritage, reflected in its legacy of having British Board Directors for over 150 years, until 1988. Further, it is a timely and strategic appointment that aligns well with the Group’s renewed vision and focus on expanding its global footprint. 

Dauris becomes the fourth Independent Non-Executive Director on the Board, and his appointment reaffirms the Company’s commitment to strong corporate governance. The increased representation of independent directors reflects George Steuart’s commitment to independent oversight, broader perspectives in Board deliberations and sound decision-making in the interests of all its shareholders. 

Commenting on the appointment, Group Chairman Sarva Ameresekere said: “We are honoured to welcome James to the Board. We believe his vast international experience and understanding of Sri Lanka will be valuable as we strive to explore opportunities beyond our shores. His addition to the Board adds further depth and diversity of expertise to support the Group’s growth aspirations.”

Speaking on his appointment, Dauris said, “I am delighted to be joining the George Steuart board at an exciting time for the Group as it works to grow its businesses in and outside Sri Lanka.  It is going to be an important period for each of the George Steuart companies and I am looking forward to helping the Board to make decisions that will serve customers, employees and shareholders well going forwards.”

Founded in 1835 by Captain James Steuart, the Group has evolved from Sri Lanka’s oldest mercantile establishment into a diversified group with interests spanning tea exports, healthcare, travel and leisure, financial services, consumer products and industrial solutions. 

The existing Board comprises Group Chairman Sarva Ameresekere, Independent Directors Devaka Cooray, Dimantha Seneviratne, Dr. Dinesh Palipana and Samantha Ranatunga, and Directors Varuni Fernando, Eran Ranasinghe, Dai Pathmanathan, Manoj Pilimatalawwe and Channe Wijemanne.

title: Tea output rebounds in October | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 03:56
-     - 22

Sri Lanka’s tea production edged up 0.37% year-on-year to 22.07 MnKg in October. A sharp recovery in High Grown and Medium Grown output offset a decline in Low Grown teas, John Keells PLC said yesterday, citing Sri Lanka Tea Board data.

Output was 0.08 MnKg above October 2025 and 0.79 MnKg, or 3.71%, above October 2024. “Sri Lanka’s tea production in October was close to last year’s level, up 0.37%,” John Keells said.

Asia Siyaka Commodities PLC, which put October production at 22 MnKg, said output had recovered from 20.27 MnKg in September. “This marks a reversal of the three-month year-on-year declining trend, which had largely been attributed to adverse weather conditions affecting production,” Asia Siyaka said.

High Grown production rose 16.65% to 4.47 MnKg, while Medium Grown output climbed 22.19% to 4.2 MnKg, John Keells said. The rebound followed a September in which excessive rainfall and poor growing conditions pushed High Grown output down to 3.49 MnKg, its lowest level since 1992, according to Asia Siyaka.

Low Grown production fell 8.98% to 13.24 MnKg, bringing its share of the crop down to 60%. Green Tea output fell 7.39% to 0.16 MnKg.

By manufacture, orthodox production rose 0.49%, while CTC (crush, tear, curl) output was level at 2.12 MnKg. Within orthodox, High Grown production rose 19.39% and Medium Grown 26.41%, while Low Grown orthodox fell 9.32%.

Cumulative production for January to October totalled 214.82 MnKg, down 2.86% from 221.15 MnKg in the same period of 2025 and 1.53% below 2024, John Keells said. Asia Siyaka said this was the lowest output for the first 10 months since 2022, when production stood at 211.7 MnKg. Total production for the whole of 2022 was 251.8 MnKg.

Medium Grown teas recorded the steepest decline over the 10 months, falling 5.76% to 36.97 MnKg. Low Grown production fell 2.58% to 130.51 MnKg and High Grown 1.57% to 45.25 MnKg, while Green Tea rose 5.49% to 2.09 MnKg.

CTC production for the period was up 3.38%, driven mainly by a 13.01% rise in Medium Grown CTC, John Keells said. Orthodox output was down 3.58%, with Medium Grown orthodox down 10.17%.

title: DFCC Bank advances core business growth, expands banking franchise | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 03:56
-     - 20

Chairman J. Durairatnam, Director and CEO Thimal Perera

DFCC Bank yesterday said it posted continued growth across its core banking businesses during the nine months ended 30 September 2026, supported by expanding lending and deposit portfolios, stronger income generation and improving asset quality.

The bank’s loan portfolio grew by 18% to Rs. 610 billion, while customer deposits increased by 23% to Rs. 694 billion compared with 31 December 2025. Total assets expanded by 13% to Rs. 965 billion. Net Interest Income increased by 8% to Rs. 24.8 billion, while Net Fee and Commission Income grew by 23% to Rs. 6.5 billion compared with the corresponding period of 2025.

Growth across these core banking businesses contributed to a Group Profit After Tax (PAT) Rs.

7.6 billion for the nine-month period. Although this was 12% below the corresponding period of 2025, the bank recorded an 18% expansion in its loan portfolio, 23% growth in deposits and a 31% increase in CASA balances compared with December 2025, while the net Stage 3 impaired loan ratio improved to 3.44% from 4.55%. These results demonstrate the continued expansion of the bank’s franchise, with a clear focus on converting greater scale and stronger income streams into sustainable profitability.

A major strategic milestone during the third quarter was the completion of DFCC Bank’s acquisition of Standard Chartered Bank PLC’s Wealth and Retail Banking business in Sri Lanka. The transaction broadened the bank’s customer base and strengthened its retail banking, cards, deposits and wealth management capabilities. The bank remains focused on maintaining service continuity, building customer confidence and realising the opportunities created by its enlarged franchise.

The bank maintained a prudent approach to credit risk, strengthening impairment provisions through refinements to its credit risk models and specific management overlays in response to prevailing economic and geopolitical uncertainties. Impairment charges increased by 10% compared with the corresponding period of 2025. Operating expenses also reflected investments in technology, customer service and the expanded workforce following the acquisition. These measures support the bank’s commitment to sound risk management and disciplined, sustainable growth.

Alongside its expanded franchise, DFCC Bank continued to improve accessibility and customer experience. During the quarter, the bank introduced an ATM and Cash Recycler Machine experience offering transactions in eight languages at Bandaranaike International Airport and selected tourism destinations. It also continued to develop customer propositions across cards, housing finance, pensioner banking and women’s entrepreneurship, including DFCC Aloka, while strengthening transaction banking and trade-related services.

The bank’s progress was also reflected in external recognition across customer service, transaction banking, people development and financial performance. These achievements, together with its expanded capabilities, reinforce DFCC Bank’s focus on deepening customer relationships, maintaining financial discipline and translating business growth into long-term value for customers, employees and shareholders.

DFCC Bank PLC, the largest entity within the group, reported a PBT of Rs. 8,736 million and a PAT of Rs. 7,323 million from core operations for the period ended 30 September 2026, compared to a PBT of Rs. 12,151 million and a PAT of Rs. 8,328 million in the corresponding period of 2025.

At group level, for the period ended 30 September 2026, PBT was Rs. 9,130 million and PAT was Rs. 7,567 million, compared to Rs. 12,480 million and Rs. 8,530 million, respectively, in 2025. The bank’s Earnings Per Share (EPS) from core banking operations was Rs. 16.38 for the period ended 30 September 2026.

The bank’s Return on Assets (ROA) before tax was 1.2%, while Return on Equity (ROE) after tax stood at 8.68% for the period ended 30 September 2026.

The bank’s total tax expense, including Value Added Tax (VAT) on financial services, Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL) on financial services, and Income Tax, amounted to Rs. 4,727 million for the period ended 30 September 2026. Consequently, the bank’s tax expense as a percentage of operating profit stood at 39% for the period.

The bank maintained its revised deposit and lending rates during the period in line with prevailing market conditions and the Central Bank of Sri Lanka’s Overnight Policy Rate. Consequently, Net Interest Income increased by 8% to Rs. 24,770 million, supported by disciplined margin management, effective balance sheet optimisation, and continued growth in earning assets. The bank’s asset base expanded by 13% over the past twelve months, while the loan portfolio recorded 23% growth compared with 30 September 2025, reflecting a strategic focus on quality asset expansion and sustainable business growth.

The bank also strengthened its funding profile, with the CASA portfolio increasing by 31% compared to 31 December 2025, resulting in the CASA ratio improving to 26.15% as at 30 September 2026. The higher contribution from CASA deposits supported funding cost optimisation and contributed positively to Net Interest Income. Despite a competitive interest rate environment and prevailing market dynamics, the bank maintained a healthy Net Interest Margin of 3.64%, underscoring the effectiveness of its prudent funding, pricing, and balance sheet management strategies.

Strategic focus on trade-related commissions and card-based services continued to drive strong growth in fee-based income, further enhanced by the successful integration of the SCB retail banking portfolio, which expanded the bank’s credit card customer base and transaction volumes. The growth in card-based activity and trade-related services contributed significantly to the overall increase in fee income during the period.

While fee-related expenses increased in line with customer acquisition, portfolio expansion, and higher transaction volumes, the overall impact remained positive. Consequently, Net Fee and Commission Income increased by 23% to Rs. 6,508 million, compared to Rs. 5,281 million in the corresponding period of 2025.

The net Stage 3 impaired loan ratio improved to 3.44% as at 30 September 2026, from 4.55% as at 31 December 2025, supported by recoveries and portfolio expansion.

In response to current and potential future impacts of global and domestic economic conditions on the bank’s lending portfolio, management strengthened impairment provisioning during the period. This was achieved through enhancements to internal expected credit loss models to capture risk factors not fully observable in the current volatile geopolitical and economic environment, including the recognition of additional provisions as management overlays for exposures to higher-risk sectors and specific customer segments, making additional provision for specific large group exposures.

The bank also maintained adequate provisioning in line with the accelerated growth in its lending portfolio. As a result, impairment charges increased to Rs. 4,807 million for the period ended 30 September 2026, compared to Rs. 4,367 million recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. These provisions have been established to safeguard the bank’s financial strength and reflect a more conservative assessment of potential credit risks, considering prevailing macroeconomic conditions and the potential impact of the geopolitical environment.

Technology and digital transformation remained key strategic priorities for the Bank during the period, supported by continued investments in IT infrastructure aimed at enhancing digital capabilities, strengthening information security, improving operational efficiency, and delivering a seamless customer experience across multiple channels. The bank also increased its investment in marketing and business development initiatives to strengthen brand visibility, deepen customer engagement, and support growth across key business segments. These investments are expected to generate long-term value by reinforcing the Bank’s market position, expanding its customer franchise, and enhancing its competitive advantage in an evolving financial services landscape.

Operating expenses were further impacted by higher card-related costs associated with increased transaction volumes and the expansion of card operations following the integration of the SCB retail banking portfolio. In addition, personnel expenses increased due to annual salary revisions, performance-based incentive payments, and the absorption of employees as part of the acquisition, reflecting the bank’s commitment to supporting growth while attracting, retaining, and rewarding talent.

As a result of these strategic growth initiatives and personnel-related costs, total operating expenses for the period ended 30 September 2026 increased to Rs. 16,906 million from Rs. 13,348 million in the corresponding period of 2025. Notwithstanding these investments, the bank remains focused on maintaining prudent cost discipline and driving operational efficiencies to support sustainable growth, profitability, and long-term shareholder value.

Total assets increased by Rs. 107 billion, representing a 13% growth compared to 31 December 2025, primarily driven by the expansion of the bank’s loan portfolio and the successful acquisition of the Wealth and Retail Banking Business of SCB. The loan book grew by Rs. 94 billion to Rs. 610 billion from Rs. 516 billion as at 31 December 2025, reflecting an 18% increase during the period.

This performance highlights the successful execution of DFCC Bank’s strategic growth initiatives, combining strong organic business expansion with the benefits of the portfolio acquisition, while maintaining a disciplined lending approach focused on asset quality and sustainable growth. The continued recovery in economic activity and improving business confidence further supported credit demand, reinforcing the bank’s role in facilitating prudent credit expansion and contributing to national economic development.

The bank’s total liabilities increased by Rs. 105 billion, reflecting a 14% growth from December 2025. The deposit base expanded by 23%, rising by Rs. 129 billion to Rs. 694 billion, up from Rs. 565 billion as at 31 December 2025, resulting in a loan-to-deposit ratio of 95.51%. Additionally, the CASA ratio stood at 26.15% as at 30 September 2026.

The bank effectively contained funding costs by utilising medium- to long-term concessionary credit lines, which supported the expansion of the lending portfolio and provided concessionary funding to customers. Factoring in these term borrowings, the CASA ratio further improved to 29.95%, while the loan-to-deposit ratio improved to 90.56% as at 30 September 2026.

As at 30 September 2026, total equity was Rs. 110 billion, supported by a profit after tax of Rs. 7.3 billion and movements across the bank’s securities portfolios.

In alignment with the bank’s growth strategy and the improving economic environment, the loan portfolio grew by 18%. Leveraging the strengthened equity base, the bank effectively absorbed the additional capital requirements associated with portfolio growth. The Tier 1 Capital Ratio was maintained at 10.437%, while the Total Capital Ratio stood at 14.017%, compared to 13.550% and 15.933%, respectively, as at 31 December 2025.

The bank’s Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) stood at 129.88%, and the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) – all currency – stood at 169.46%, both comfortably exceeding regulatory minimums.

Director/CEO Thimal Perera said: DFCC Bank continued to grow its core businesses during the nine months ended 30 September 2026. Loans increased by 18% to Rs. 610 billion and deposits by 23% to Rs. 694 billion from 31 December 2025. Total assets grew by 13% to Rs. 965 billion. Net Interest Income rose by 8% to Rs. 24.8 billion and Net Fee and Commission Income by 23% to Rs. 6.5 billion against the corresponding period of 2025. Group PAT was Rs. 7.6 billion, 12% lower year on year. The net Stage 3 impaired loan ratio improved to 3.44% from 4.55% at year-end.

CEO/Director Thimal Perera said: “We strengthened impairment provisions through credit risk model refinements and management overlays, while continuing to invest in people, technology and operating capacity. Capital and liquidity remained above regulatory requirements. Our focus is to convert greater scale and stronger customer relationships into sustainable earnings, with disciplined judgement on risk and costs.

“The acquisition of Standard Chartered Bank’s Wealth and Retail Banking business brought approximately 50,000 customer accounts and around 260 colleagues into DFCC Bank, expanding our network and strengthening our retail and wealth capabilities. Completion was an important milestone; the real test is whether customers continue to feel well served and our new colleagues feel that they belong and can contribute. We are working to preserve trusted customer relationships and build one stronger team.”

 “We will convert our increased scale into stronger relationships, better customer experiences and sustainable performance, while managing credit quality, capital, liquidity and costs with care. I thank our customers, colleagues, shareholders, regulators and partners for their continued trust and support. We move forward with broader capabilities and a responsibility to deepen our contribution to Sri Lanka.”

title: Public sector 312,626 short of approved cadre | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 03:55
-     - 19

The public sector continues to function under capacity with an actual cadre of 1,028,861 as at 30 June, 2026, against an approved cadre of 1,341,487. That leaves 312,626 posts, or 23.3%, unfilled, according to a Department of Management Services report released on 12 November, 2026.

The ‘Cadre Information of the Public Sector 2026’ report was issued under the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development. “In terms of Section 20(2)(g) of the Public Financial Management Act No. 44 of 2024, a summary of public service employment across budgetary entities is required to be submitted along with the Annual Budget Document,” the report said.

The public service, which excludes State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), had 893,797 employees against 1,130,764 approved posts, a shortfall of 236,967 or 21%. Ministries and departments made up 135,874 of the vacancies, with 458,074 employees against 593,948 approved posts. Provincial Councils were closest to full strength, at 386,429 employees or 84.2% of their approved 459,166. District and Divisional Secretariats stood at 71.6% of approved cadre.

Budget 2027, presented on the same day, allocates Rs. 1.41 trillion for public sector salaries and wages in 2027. That is up from Rs. 1.29 trillion in the revised estimates for 2026 and Rs. 1.16 trillion in 2025, and amounts to 23.7% of total recurrent expenditure of Rs. 5.94 trillion.

The 2027 Appropriation Bill also allocates Rs. 550 billion to the Department of Pensions, up from Rs. 489 billion in 2026. Together, salaries, wages and pensions account for about a third of the Government’s recurrent spending. Excluding interest payments of Rs. 2.64 trillion, the share rises to nearly 60%. The Budget also proposes Rs. 34.8 billion for higher allowances for the tri-forces, Police and prisons, and Rs. 4 billion for an interim allowance for 2020-2024 pensioners.

Special Spending Units were at 44.3% of approved cadre, with 10,218 employees against 23,082 approved posts. The Judicial Service Commission pulled that figure down most, reporting 5,256 employees against 15,058 approved posts. The report also gives no actual cadre for the Presidential Secretariat, which has 1,130 approved posts.

The gap was wider among Central Government SOEs, which had 131,902 employees against 206,162 approved posts, a 36% shortfall. However, the approved figure includes 26,783 posts at the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB), for which the report lists no actual cadre. “According to the Sri Lanka Electricity Act No. 36 of 2024, the cadre of the Ceylon Electricity Board was transferred to the successor companies of the Ceylon Electricity Board,” the report said. Without the CEB, the SOE shortfall comes to 47,477 posts, or 26.5%. Provincial Council SOEs had 3,162 employees against 4,561 approved posts.

The largest single gap was at the Ministry of Public Security and Parliamentary Affairs, which had 120,753 employees against 169,525 approved posts, 48,772 short. Within it, the Sri Lanka Police uniformed cadre stood at 73,875 against 102,112 approved, and the Department of Civil Security at 30,046 against 40,183.

The Ministry of Education, Higher Education and Vocational Education, including its SOEs, was 33,570 short, with 96,065 employees against 129,635 approved posts. National Schools alone had 52,434 employees against 69,004 approved. The Ministry of Health and Mass Media was 31,114 short, at 110,396 against 141,510. Within that ministry, the Department of Posts had 19,490 employees against 27,018 approved posts.

Among ministries with more than 50,000 approved posts, the Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, Land and Irrigation had the highest vacancy rate, at 29.7%, with 46,869 employees against 66,681 approved. Under the Ministry of Transport, Highways and Urban Development, the Department of Sri Lanka Railways had 14,554 employees against 20,650 approved posts.

The revenue agencies were also understaffed. Sri Lanka Customs had 2,238 employees against 3,148 approved posts, the Department of Inland Revenue 2,409 against 2,910 and the Department of Excise 1,230 against 1,720.

The figures by staff category exclude Central Government SOEs, which the report does not break down by category. Activity in the country’s manufacturing and services sectors expanded at a faster pace in October, according to the Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) released yesterday by its compiler, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL).

The PMI is based on a monthly survey of businesses. A reading above the neutral threshold of 50 shows expansion compared with the previous month, and a reading below 50 shows contraction.

The Manufacturing PMI rose to 55.3 in October from 53 in September. The CBSL said the expansion was broad-based, with all sub-indices above the neutral threshold. However, the index was still below the 61 recorded in October 2025.

The New Orders sub-index rose to 55 from 51. The CBSL said the increase was driven by the textiles and wearing apparel and the food and beverages sectors, reflecting seasonal demand. Production rose to 52.2 from 51, also driven by seasonal demand in the textiles and wearing apparel sector.

Employment continued to expand, although at a slower pace, with the sub-index easing to 51.1 from 52.6. Stock of Purchases rose to 56.1 from the neutral 50 recorded in September, in line with the growth in New Orders and Production. Meanwhile, Suppliers’ Delivery Time lengthened further, with the sub-index rising to 66.1 from 63, reflecting increased demand for inputs.

The CBSL said the outlook for manufacturing activities over the next three months is favourable, underpinned by anticipated demand during the upcoming festive season.

The Services PMI, measured by the Business Activity Index, rose to 62.5 in October from 60.5 in September, indicating that services activities expanded at a higher rate. The index was below the 66 recorded in October 2025.

Business Activity was driven primarily by improvements in other personal services, with notable contributions from financial services and goods transportation.

New Businesses continued to grow, although at a slower pace, with the sub-index easing to 59.8 from 60.9. According to the CBSL, the growth mainly reflected expansion in financial services and other personal services, alongside positive contributions from accommodation, food and beverage services, and transportation of goods.

Services Employment rose to 56.1 from 54, supported by recruitment across several sub-sectors to meet rising operational requirements. Meanwhile, Backlogs of Work declined at a faster rate, with the sub-index falling to 48.1 from 49.4.

Expectations for Business Activity over the next three months stayed positive, although the sub-index eased to 74.7 from 76.2. The CBSL said expectations were supported by favourable macroeconomic conditions, anticipated increases in tourist arrivals and the upcoming festive season. However, it warned that prevailing global uncertainties continue to pose downside risks to the outlook.

Sri Lanka’s expansion comes as PMIs in major economies continue to rise. The CBSL release cites S&P Global data as of 16 November, 2026. On that data, manufacturing activity was rising at a slower rate globally and in India, China, the US and the Eurozone, and at a higher rate in the UK. Services activity was rising at a slower rate globally and in China, the US and the Eurozone, and at a higher rate in India and the UK.

title: 2027 Budget: AI audit that audited itself | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 04:52
-     - 11

Soon after the Budget Speech 2027 was tabled, a social media post landed in my feed claiming the document was full of arithmetic errors and other mistakes. I wanted to test that claim myself. So I uploaded the full English text to an AI tool and asked it a blunt question: find the mistakes.

It took less than 30 seconds. The list read like the opening of a scandal. A Rs. 1.5 billion arithmetic error in the minor-irrigation allocations. MSME loan schemes worth Rs. 140 billion inflated to Rs. 174 billion. A nine-month primary surplus of Rs. 1,844 billion that the tool called mathematically impossible. A World Bank upgrade to upper-middle-income status that, it claimed, never happened. A primary expenditure projection of 13.6% of GDP that broke the 13% ceiling in the Public Financial Management Act.

I had a social media post drafted within minutes. The angle wrote itself. A government that had just allocated Rs. 28,500 million for the digital economy, and announced a National Artificial Intelligence Centre of Excellence, had senior officials who couldn’t spend 30 seconds running their own document through basic AI.

Then I checked each claim against the speech and public data. The draft went in the bin.

What the machine got wrong

The Rs. 1.5 billion error came first. The speech lists four minor-irrigation allocations: Rs. 2,000 million to the Department of Agrarian Development, Rs. 7,500 million for Provincial Council tanks, anicuts and canals, Rs. 2,500 million under the “Wari Mahimaya - Ape Urumaya” program, and Rs. 1,500 million for schemes damaged by Cyclone Ditwah. They add to Rs. 13,500 million. The next sentence reads: “Including these, around Rs. 15,000 million has been allocated directly for the maintenance and development of minor irrigation schemes.”

Including these. The total covers the four named items plus other spending. The AI read a subset as a sum and manufactured a Rs. 1.5 billion hole.

The MSME figure failed the same way. Rs. 174 billion is the volume of concessionary loans the Treasury expects State and private banks to issue, backed by Rs. 67,687 million in interest subsidies and refinancing. The speech says this total “includes the following loan schemes.” A partial list was again treated as the full bill.

The primary surplus claim was weaker still. Central Bank data reported in June showed a primary surplus of Rs. 1.13 trillion in the first five months of 2026. Revenue and grants reached Rs. 5,485.6 billion in 2025. A Rs. 1,844 billion surplus by September is large, and the end-year target of Rs. 360 billion tells you spending is loaded into the final quarter. It is entirely possible.

The World Bank claim was flatly false. On 1 July 2026 the Bank reclassified Sri Lanka as upper-middle-income, with Atlas GNI per capita of $4,670 against a threshold of $4,636. Dr. W.A. Wijewardena wrote about that narrow $34 margin in July. Every major Sri Lankan outlet carried the news.

The fiscal law claim read only half the law. The PFM Act caps primary expenditure at 13% of GDP, and it also contains an escape clause for exceptional events. The Government activated that clause after Cyclone Ditwah, when the Rs. 500 billion supplementary estimate pushed 2026 primary expenditure to 13.7% of GDP. The 2027 speech projects 13.6% as a temporary increase and commits to returning to 13% from 2028.

What it got right

One finding survived. In the rural roads section, allocations of Rs. 55,000 million for rural roads and bridges, Rs. 5,500 million for rural bridges and Rs. 20,000 million for Provincial Council roads add to Rs. 80,500 million. The speech then refers to “the aforementioned Rs. 80,000 million.” That is a Rs. 500 million slip. It is real and worth correcting, and a long way from the Rs. 1.5 billion headline the tool handed me.

A legitimate policy debate also sits behind the false “illegal” claim. Using the escape clause in two consecutive years tests the credibility of a ceiling that Verité Research has already described as the most extreme of its kind in the world. That debate deserves serious analysis, built on what the law actually says.

Why this should worry the people spending Rs. 28.5 b

Language models predict plausible text. Plausible and correct overlap most of the time, which is exactly why the gaps are dangerous. When the tool scanned the budget speech, it did what a pattern-matcher does: it found numbers near a total and assumed they should add up. It skipped the word “including.” It appears to have leaned on outdated information about Sri Lanka’s income status from before July 2026. Then it delivered every guess in the same confident tone as the one real error.

Had I posted the original draft, I would have accused public servants of sloppiness using claims far sloppier than anything in the speech. A share-hungry audience would have carried it. The correction would have arrived days later and reached a fraction of those readers.

The post that sent me looking may well have started the same way: an AI summary, read once, shared without a second check.

The budget’s digital agenda now has to manage exactly this risk. The speech commits money to digital government transformation, a Cyber Security Authority and an AI Centre of Excellence at Wijerama. Those investments will put AI tools in the hands of thousands of officials drafting procurement papers, policy notes and, eventually, budget documents.

Access to the tools is the easy part. Verification is the bottleneck. An official who pastes a document into an AI tool and forwards the output has gained speed and lost accountability. An official who uses the tool to generate a list of questions, then checks each one against the source, keeps both.

A rule worth adopting

The Treasury could set one simple standard before the first Presidential Digital Excellence Award is handed out: every AI-assisted finding in an official document carries a human-verified source reference. A page number, a table or a dataset. No reference, no inclusion.

The same rule applies to the rest of us. Business owners, journalists and consultants, myself included, will use AI to read budgets, annual reports and contracts faster than ever. The 30 seconds I saved on the first read cost me an hour on the second, and that hour was the difference between an embarrassing post and an accurate one.

AI found the questions in Budget 2027. People still have to find the answers.

(The author is Founder and CEO of INOTREND Int., a neuromarketing and behavioural strategy consultancy, and CIM UK Brand Ambassador for Sri Lanka)

title: PSTA: Still in violation of international norms | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 04:30
-     - 21

It is the job of the Government, not of the Supreme Court, to ensure that Bills are consistent with international norms set out in international conventions that Sri Lanka has ratified, such as the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). The Court’s determination on the Protection of the State against Terrorism Bill (PSTA) only addressed questions of consistency with the Constitution, based on some curious rationalisations. That is within the authority of the Court.

In its determination, the Court did not mandate any changes to section 27 that empowers the Secretary of the Ministry to issue detention orders nor change the word “shall” to “may” in section 26(3), preserving the ability of the Executive to deprive a person of liberty without judicial oversight. The review committee established under section 30 was mentioned in positive tone, without proposing any changes to its appointment by the Minister without Constitutional Council concurrence and its powers being only recommendatory (section 30(8)). The broad powers given to the President to indefinitely proscribe organisation were discussed but no material changes were mandated.

This leaves it up to the Executive, headed by the President, to make the necessary changes. Indeed, the President has stated that the Government will consult with civil society on the PSTA and on the even worse Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill (POCA). The Bills cannot be taken up by Parliament until the budget debate has been concluded in any case.

Minimum changes

The Government should use this window to listen to the reasoned arguments that have been made and make the necessary changes on political and economic grounds. They have already paid the political price for reneging on an explicit manifesto promise. They may be able to remedy part of the damage by making changes even at this late stage. The economic reasons are much stronger. The GSP+ application is endangered by the Bill in its current form. It can be denied if Sri Lanka retains the Prevention of Terrorism Act or enacts new law that does not meet the norms set out in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) that Sri Lanka acceded to on 11 June 1980.

The Executive should step back from the insistence that the decision to incarcerate a person suspected of having committed an offence under the PSTA for up to two months is its alone and does not involve the judicial branch. The Government does not appear to trust Magistrates with decisions on granting bail. Perhaps the decisions to detain a person should also be moved up the judicial hierarchy to the High Court and out of the Executive. This action will make the PSTA compliant with ICCPR Article 9(3).

The requirement of an appeal of a detention order under ICCPR Article 9(4) may be met easily. The review committee proposed in section 30(4) should be made truly independent and its decisions final. Independence can be strengthened by having the Constitutional Council approve the appointments. Amendment of section 30(8) removing the powers of the Minister to disregard the committee’s recommendations will complete the remediation.

The most puzzling aspect of the Supreme Court’s determination is that relating to the President’s untrammeled powers to proscribe organisations (section 59). Article 155 of the Constitution allows the Executive to take urgent measures under the Public Security Ordinance (No. 25 of 1947) but requires Parliament to concur every month. As the Court notes, it may be necessary to take prompt action on terrorist organisations. That is the purpose of the Public Security Ordinance.

Why the Court has allowed the Constitutional safeguard on the actions of the Executive in conditions of exception to be bypassed is puzzling. While this may not directly affect GSP+, it is hoped that the Government will reconsider giving the President the power to proscribe without the involvement (even after a month) of the legislature. Merely substituting the Supreme Court for the Court of Appeals does not cure the harm caused by granting of sole authority to the President.

Avoiding the core issues

The Presidency is a political position. From the time of the 17th Amendment, the trend has been to introduce checks and balances on the enormous powers granted the President by the original 1978 Constitution. An organisation that has been unjustly proscribed by the President is asked to appeal to the Supreme Court instead of the Court of Appeals, as though that is a practical solution in that the organisation is unable to use its own resources even to launch the appeal because its bank accounts are frozen by the proscription order. In the same way that the addition of a phrase to section 29(2) does not remedy the core problem of the Executive depriving persons of liberty, this too makes changes at the margin, without addressing the core issue.

title: Seven decades of Budgets, one unbroken economic failure: Can Sri Lanka finally escape its past? | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 04:26
-     - 20

From Bandaranaike’s State-led economy to Jayewardene’s liberalisation, Rajapaksa’s infrastructure ambitions and Dissanayake’s fiscal discipline, successive Governments have promised prosperity through competing economic models. Sri Lanka’s 2027 Budget proposes an ambitious transition from stabilisation to development. But does it address the institutional failures that have repeatedly prevented economic recovery from becoming lasting prosperity?

Sri Lanka’s 2027 Budget arrives at an extraordinary moment in the country’s economic history. Four years after sovereign default, foreign reserves have recovered, Government revenue has strengthened and economic growth has returned. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake can reasonably point to an economy considerably more stable than the one that collapsed in 2022. Yet stability, however necessary, is not transformation. The consequential question is whether this Budget represents a fundamental restructuring of Sri Lanka’s economy or another restoration of financial order within a system whose underlying weaknesses remain unresolved. For a country that has repeatedly mistaken economic recovery for lasting development, the distinction is neither academic nor insignificant.

For nearly seven decades, Sri Lanka’s budgets have reflected competing economic philosophies, each promising to overcome the limitations of its predecessor. Yet beneath those ideological differences lies a remarkable continuity: successive administrations have struggled to convert public expenditure, economic reform and periods of growth into sustainable productive capacity. Governments have repeatedly changed the relationship between the State and the market without sufficiently strengthening the institutions responsible for directing investment, enforcing accountability and delivering results. This recurring institutional weakness, rather than the failure of any single ideology, provides the historical context against which the 2027 Budget must be judged.

Seven decades of economic promises and recurring structural weaknesses

The Bandaranaike era marked an expansion of State intervention, reflecting postcolonial ambitions to strengthen domestic ownership and reduce dependence on foreign commercial interests. Sirimavo Bandaranaike’s administrations subsequently deepened nationalisation, import substitution and State-led industrial development. These policies emerged from legitimate concerns about sovereignty and inequality, while Sri Lanka’s broader welfare commitments contributed to important achievements in education and healthcare. Nevertheless, extensive protection, foreign exchange restrictions and administrative controls constrained investment and competition. The World Bank subsequently cited estimates suggesting that economic distortions during 1971–77 reduced annual growth by approximately two percentage points. The lesson was not that public intervention was inherently misguided, but that ownership and protection alone could not guarantee productive efficiency.

Sri Lanka has learned how to survive an economic crisis. The greater challenge is proving that it has learned how not to create another

J.R. Jayewardene’s 1977 liberalisation represented an ideological reversal. Trade restrictions were relaxed, foreign investment encouraged and export manufacturing expanded, with the garment industry demonstrating the possibilities of international integration. Yet liberalisation did not establish sufficiently diversified industrial capabilities, while civil war imposed enormous fiscal costs. The post-war period under Mahinda Rajapaksa subsequently promoted infrastructure-led growth, financed partly through external borrowing. Roads, ports and energy facilities improved connectivity, but the commercial returns and financing of individual projects raised questions about sustainability. Following Gotabaya Rajapaksa’s 2019 tax reductions, which the IMF estimated cost more than 2% of GDP in revenue, existing vulnerabilities intensified. Combined with pandemic disruptions, debt pressures and serious policy failures, the consequences culminated in the 2022 collapse. Across these competing models, Sri Lanka repeatedly failed to establish the institutional discipline necessary for sustainable development.

Fiscal recovery is measurable. But whatW does the 2027 Budget actually change?

Against this history, Dissanayake’s fiscal achievements deserve recognition. According to the Budget Speech, Government revenue increased from 8.2% of GDP in 2022 to 16.6% in 2025, while the overall deficit narrowed to 2.3% of GDP in 2025. Economic growth reached 5%. Nevertheless, stabilisation began under the IMF-supported program negotiated during Ranil Wickremesinghe’s presidency. The NPP Government deserves credit for maintaining fiscal continuity despite its earlier opposition to aspects of the prevailing economic framework. Pragmatism need not indicate ideological weakness, but it raises an important question: what distinguishes the administration’s promised transformation from the recovery program it inherited?

The 2027 estimates project revenue of Rs 6.15 trillion against expenditure of Rs 7.673 trillion, rising to Rs 7.933 trillion with supplementary expenditure. Interest payments alone amount to Rs 2.643 trillion, exceeding the underlying public-investment allocation of Rs 1.75 trillion. The Government projects a primary surplus of Rs 1.15 trillion before supplementary expenditure, demonstrating fiscal restraint but also the limited resources available for development after financing existing obligations. The proposed Rs 2 trillion public-investment program includes supplementary reconstruction funding associated with Cyclone Ditwah. Reconstruction is necessary, but restoring damaged assets must not be confused with creating entirely new productive capacity.

The more revealing concern is implementation. The IMF reported that capital expenditure was under-executed by approximately 1% of GDP annually during 2023–25. This suggests that stronger fiscal balances have partly coincided with the State’s inability to execute planned development expenditure. The Government’s new investment commitments therefore require independently evaluated feasibility studies, transparent procurement, published implementation schedules and measurable economic returns. Without these safeguards, Sri Lanka risks repeating a familiar pattern in which announcements acquire greater political importance than completed projects.

The transport proposals illustrate both opportunities and difficult choices. The Budget allocates Rs 80 billion towards the first phase of suburban railway electrification, including the Kelani Valley, Main and Coastal lines, while proposing Rs 30 billion for the Kurunegala–Galewela Expressway section and Rs 27 billion for the Ruwanpura Expressway. Railway electrification could reduce dependence on imported fuel, improve commuting efficiency and increase productivity if accompanied by reliable services and affordable fares. Expressways may improve freight movement and regional connectivity, but their benefits depend upon traffic demand, maintenance costs and integration with productive economic activity. The relevant question is not whether infrastructure generates visible development, but whether each rupee invested produces greater economic value than alternative uses of limited public funds.

The real achievement of this Budget will not be determined by the size of its allocations, the elegance of its projections or the confidence of its parliamentary presentation. It will be determined by whether the economy emerging from recovery is fundamentally stronger than the one that failed

Taxation, agriculture and the distribution of economic opportunity

The Budget proposes increasing the monthly personal income tax-free threshold from Rs 150,000 to Rs 162,500 and revising progressive tax brackets. These changes provide relief to sections of the formal workforce, while the proposed VAT exemption for printed books and exercise books recognises educational affordability. However, the projected Rs 3.592 trillion in taxes on goods and services, compared with Rs 1.341 trillion from income taxes, demonstrates continued reliance on consumption taxation. This raises substantial distributional concerns because lower-income households spend larger proportions of their incomes on necessities, while personal income tax concessions primarily benefit those above the tax threshold. A credible progressive fiscal framework must assess not merely revenue collection but who ultimately finances recovery.

The World Bank estimates that poverty remained at 16.9% in 2025, compared with 11.5% in 2019. Against this backdrop, the Rs 230 billion allocation for social protection allowances, including Aswesuma, and increases in monthly allowances for people with disabilities and kidney disease from Rs 10,000 to Rs 12,500 address genuine hardship. The additional Rs 25 billion for the Praja Shakthi rural development program could strengthen local economic opportunity. Yet welfare must be connected to employment, education and productive capital. Otherwise, transfers may alleviate immediate deprivation without addressing the conditions that reproduce poverty.

Agriculture offers a particularly revealing example of the structural challenge. The Budget acknowledges that the sector employs approximately 23.9% of the workforce while contributing only around 8.4% of economic output. Its Rs 44 billion fertiliser subsidy, supporting payments of Rs 30,000 per hectare, may reduce production costs, but subsidies alone cannot resolve low productivity, fragmented cultivation or weaknesses in marketing. The proposed collective Yaya production system, improved agricultural service centres and greater flexibility in cultivating underutilised paddy lands could improve efficiency. Their success, however, depends upon farmer participation, market access, water management and fair pricing. Sri Lanka must move beyond measuring agricultural policy through subsidies distributed and begin evaluating productivity, farmer incomes and value added per hectare.

The Rs 67.687 billion allocated for enterprise lending subsidies and refinancing, intended to support approximately Rs 174 billion in concessionary loans, represents another potentially significant intervention. Affordable credit could help small enterprises recover from the crisis, acquire machinery and expand employment. Yet lending is not synonymous with productive investment. Banks must distinguish viable enterprises from businesses unable to repay, while policymakers should assess whether subsidised finance generates sustained income rather than temporary liquidity. Credit schemes will have limited transformational value without market access, business development services and reliable infrastructure.

For decades, Sri Lanka’s political establishment has treated economic recovery as evidence of national progress. The events of 2022 demonstrated how misleading that assumption can become

Building productive capacity: The real test of transformation

Foreign direct investment remains central to the Government’s development ambitions. The proposed 200% enhanced capital allowance for qualifying Board of Investment-approved export manufacturing and tourism investments, subject to a minimum investment of $3 million, could encourage capital formation. However, tax concessions cannot indefinitely compensate for unpredictable regulations, administrative delays, expensive energy or weak contract enforcement. Sri Lanka must examine whether investment incentives generate additional economic activity that would otherwise not occur, rather than simply reducing taxation on investments already commercially attractive.

India offers opportunities for integration into regional manufacturing, logistics, pharmaceuticals and professional services, while Vietnam demonstrates how investment policy, infrastructure and export integration can support industrial expansion. Sri Lanka cannot mechanically reproduce another country’s economic model, but it can recognise that sustainable foreign investment requires an entire ecosystem of productive capabilities. Its objective should be to generate skilled employment, domestic supplier networks and technological learning rather than merely celebrate announced investment commitments.

Energy policy is equally consequential. The Budget outlines plans to increase battery energy-storage capacity from 160 MW in 2026 to 560 MW in 2027, alongside a proposed subsidy of up to Rs 250,000 for eligible domestic rooftop solar battery systems. These measures could improve renewable-energy integration and reduce vulnerability to imported fuel, although their benefits depend upon grid reliability, competitive procurement and transparent subsidy targeting. Energy security is not simply an environmental objective: reliable and competitively priced electricity is essential for industrial competitiveness, household welfare and investor confidence.

The Government’s digitalisation agenda, including the proposed National Artificial Intelligence Centre of Excellence, expanded Government cloud infrastructure and digital public services, could similarly improve administrative efficiency. Yet digital transformation must mean more than converting inefficient procedures into electronic formats. It should reduce discretionary approvals, improve transparency and establish measurable service standards. The same principle applies to healthcare and education, where proposed investments in medical equipment, ambulances, teacher development and digital learning could strengthen human capital. Their long-term value depends upon equitable access, maintenance, professional capacity and measurable improvements in public services.

The Budget also proposes increased allowances for medical officers, nurses, university academics and other public employees, partly phased across 2027 and 2028. Such measures may help retain skilled personnel and recognise rising living costs, particularly in essential services. Nevertheless, recurrent commitments create continuing fiscal obligations. They should therefore be integrated with transparent workforce planning, performance standards and broader institutional improvements rather than treated as substitutes for reform.

The ultimate test: Has Sri Lanka changed the economy or merely its management?

External vulnerabilities remain substantial. The Budget projects foreign debt-service obligations of approximately $2.99 billion in 2027 and $3.57 billion in 2028. With the existing IMF program approaching its scheduled conclusion in March 2027, the Government must determine how stability can be sustained without recurring emergency assistance. International support may remain valuable, particularly amid geopolitical instability and climate shocks, but the ultimate measure of recovery cannot be the successful negotiation of successive rescue arrangements. It must be the development of institutions and industries capable of reducing the likelihood that another rescue becomes necessary.

The NPP’s electoral mandate makes this challenge especially consequential. Its political appeal rested substantially upon dissatisfaction with corruption, entrenched privilege and established political practices. A mandate for systemic change demands more than competent management of existing economic arrangements. It requires transparent public investment, predictable regulation, effective procurement oversight and accountability for expenditure that fails to produce intended results. These reforms may lack the visibility of major budget announcements, but their cumulative economic consequences could prove substantially greater.

The 2027 Budget contains credible proposals across infrastructure, agriculture, enterprise development, social protection, energy and human capital. Its ambitions address genuine structural weaknesses, yet the proposals remain promises until their economic effects can be demonstrated. Sri Lanka’s history offers no simple ideological solution: State-led development struggled with efficiency, liberalisation expanded opportunity without eliminating vulnerability, infrastructure investment created assets alongside financing risks, and fiscal stabilisation restored confidence without guaranteeing productive transformation.

Dissanayake now confronts the challenge that successive administrations have approached through competing economic philosophies: converting public policy into durable institutional capability and sustained prosperity. Sri Lanka has demonstrated that it can collect taxes, restrain expenditure and rebuild reserves. It has not yet demonstrated that it can consistently attract productive investment, generate sophisticated exports, create high-quality employment and distribute the gains of growth fairly.

For decades, Sri Lanka’s political establishment has treated economic recovery as evidence of national progress. The events of 2022 demonstrated how misleading that assumption can become. The real achievement of this Budget will not be determined by the size of its allocations, the elegance of its projections or the confidence of its parliamentary presentation. It will be determined by whether the economy emerging from recovery is fundamentally stronger than the one that failed.

Sri Lanka has learned how to survive an economic crisis. The greater challenge is proving that it has learned how not to create another.

(The author is an International Relations student at Monash University whose writing explores politics, governance, and international affairs)

Sri Lankan cricket fans have been denied the opportunity to witness two ICC World events due to Government interference

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

Following an ICC executive meeting in Indonesia, reports confirmed that Sri Lanka will not host any major ICC men’s tournaments through 2035.

Asian regional hosting obligations for the upcoming cycle were instead awarded to India and Bangladesh, including the 2029 Champions Trophy to India and the 2031 ODI World Cup jointly to India and Bangladesh. Furthermore, a decision was made by the ICC to grant Bangladesh and the USA hosting rights for men’s and women’s cricket qualifying tournaments for the 2028 Olympic Games.

Usually it is India and Sri Lanka who co-host ICC world tournaments. The two countries co-hosted the men’s T20 World Cup in February-March this year, a month before the present SLC Transformation Committee was appointed by the Government. They also co-hosted the Women’s Cricket World Cup (50-over) in September-November 2025.

The ICC does not recognize politically appointed administrations and strictly prohibits Government involvement in member boards.

This had resulted in Sri Lanka being stripped of hosting rights for the inaugural six-team ICC Women’s Champions Trophy in February 2027. The event was relocated to Mumbai and Vadodara in India.

Following the resignation of SLC’s elected executive committee, the Sri Lankan Government appointed an interim Transformation Committee to overhaul the board’s constitution and electoral system. Because SLC lacks an elected leadership, its representatives have been excluded from ICC board meetings.

Sri Lanka also lost the opportunity of hosting the 2024 ICC Men’s Under19 World Cup due to heavy Government and Sports Ministry interventions in SLC’s governance that resulted in an interim committee being appointed. In November 2023 the ICC re-located the tournament from Sri Lanka to South Africa.

These missed opportunities have cost Sri Lanka dearly not only with the chance of hosting ICC world events but also financially.

Losing the 2027 Women’s Champions Trophy alone represented an estimated revenue loss of roughly $ 20 million (around Rs. 6.65 billion) for SLC and the local economy, alongside a forfeited $ 2 million hosting fee.

Sri Lanka Cricket administration has been plagued by interim committees since 1999. The present Transformation Committee is expected to put things right by bringing out a new constitution that is currently pending approval in Parliament.

Dhananjaya de Silva arrives for practice ahead of the second TestM Spinners Keshara Nuwantha and Prabath Jayasuriya in the fray for a place

RAWALPINDI: The pitch prepared for the second Test between Sri Lanka and Pakistan commencing today at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium is expected to be another green top like the first but the big question is whether Sri Lanka will once again, if they win the toss, invite Pakistan to bat first.  

Like the first Test the pitch for the second is also likely to have a lot of grass covering on it, but the greenness can at times be rather misleading.

Sri Lanka always has a habit of panicking when they see green on the surface and if they happen to win the toss they are most likely to play it safe and invite the opposition to bat first. This decision can at times backfire because the pitch for all its greenness will not be as helpful to the fast bowlers as expected and eventually turn into a batting surface.

Former Australian captain Ian Chappell has frequently criticized modern captains who win the toss and blindly choose to insert the opposition to bat first. In his view it is a lack of common sense that often lets the opposition stay alive in the game rather than setting up an aggressive path to victory.

Sri Lanka inserted Pakistan in the first Test but their bowlers failed to make use of the conditions and whatever assistance the pitch offered. They managed to capture only two wickets in the first session that saw Pakistan accumulate 137 runs, which did not justify their decision to field first.

Taking at least three wickets before lunch proves that the bowling attack has successfully exploited those early conditions. In red-ball cricket, a standard morning session lasts roughly two hours or 30 overs. Losing three or more wickets in that window puts the batting side firmly on the back foot and shifts momentum to the fielding team.

But it didn’t happen that way as Pakistan were able to use the conditions to come up with a daunting first innings total of 434-9 declared that pushed Sri Lanka onto the back foot. That Sri Lanka was able to manage a slender first innings lead of 12 was due to former skipper Dhananjaya de Silva and present skipper Kusal Mendis hitting centuries apiece and figuring in a double century stand.

At the end of day 3 with Sri Lanka on 404-3 they were expected to overtake Pakistan’s total and build a big lead that could have given them a chance to push for a win. But Pakistan came back strongly on day 4 to snatch the last four Lankan wickets for 42 runs and thereafter with bad light and rain interfering the Test petered out into a draw.

What was most encouraging from Pakistan’s point was that on a fourth day pitch debutant fast bowler Saqib Khan bowled magnificently to capture five of the six wickets to fall to end with excellent figures of 7/130. Saqib in fact showed the Lankan pacers who were wayward and bowled far too short in the first innings, how to bowl on such surfaces. Although Sri Lanka’s bowlers displayed much better control of line and length in the second innings the Test was too far gone to produce a winning result.

Most impressive for Sri Lanka in the bowling line up were Asitha Fernando and bowling all-rounder Milan Rathnayaka who are most likely to retain their places for today’s game. Lahiru Kumara and Dilshan Madushanka were both disappointing. Having gone into the first Test with a four-pace attack, Sri Lanka are likely to review that combination for the second Test by including a spinner at the cost of a fast bowler. The choice is between the experienced Prabath Jayasuriya and the fast improving Keshara Nuwantha. The batting remains untouched. (ST)

title: Test Twenty makes promising start in Colombo as new format takes shape | Daily FT

Cricket has reinvented itself several times over the years, from the timeless charm of Test matches to the commercial success of T20. Now, a new format is attempting to find its place in the sun, with Colombo providing the launching pad.

Test Twenty, the brainchild of sports entrepreneur Gaurav Bahirvani, seeks to marry the tactical intrigue of Test cricket with the fast paced entertainment of the shortest format.

The concept features an 80-over contest, with each team batting twice for 20 overs, bringing the possibility of shifting fortunes and second chances within a single day’s play.

“Test Twenty was never intended to replace an existing format, but to complement cricket’s evolution and create something that appeals to the next generation,” Bahirvani said.

The inaugural tournament, being played at the SSC from November 14 to 29, features 160 players aged between 13 and 21, representing South Asia, Australasia, Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa. Perhaps its most striking innovation is the Parity Rule, which brings boys and girls under one continental banner, with their performances contributing equally towards the final result.

The initiative has attracted some heavyweight backing, with former international stars Sir Clive Lloyd, AB de Villiers and Matthew Hayden serving on its advisory board. Rajkumar Sharma, best known for mentoring Virat Kohli, chairs the selection committee.

Bahirvani believes the format could open doors for youngsters who might otherwise struggle to gain exposure.

“We wanted equality to be reflected in the way the game is played,” he said.

Whether Test Twenty can establish itself alongside cricket’s three recognised international formats remains to be seen. But its promoters believe the combination of youth development, gender equality and tactical innovation offers something different in an increasingly crowded cricket calendar.
